name: Dana Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Dana. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in-house for Northgate Homes, a housing association, so it's social housing: flats and terraces, about six thousand homes. I pick up my job list on a tablet at half seven, then it's tripping fuse boards, mouldy extractor fans, smoke alarms, the odd full rewire when a flat's empty. I love the tenants, mostly, especially the older ones who make you tea and tell you about their grandkids. What wears me out is the repeat visits, going back to the same block every month because nobody will pay to fix the root problem.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single at the moment and I live in my nan's old house, which my sister and I inherited, and I rent her half from her cheaply. I've got about nine months of money put away. I'm in the union, I'm a workplace rep for the trades, and I use ChatGPT now and then, mainly to word complaints to management so I don't sound angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the actual problems, like damp and old wiring in council flats. Online I'd probably share something saying the money spent on AI hype should have gone into housing. At work I'd mostly shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. My job's in people's homes with my hands, and that was never going to be done by a chatbot. If anything, the scheduling software might stop sending me to the wrong block twice in a morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Northgate and keep my savings ticking over. I'd probably start the heat pump and solar course I've been eyeing, because the association has a target to retrofit a thousand homes. That's where the extra work is going to be, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's my normal life, and my normal life is pretty good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said repeat visits wear you out. Would AI help with that at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. If the system could spot that flat 14 has had five call-outs for the same circuit, someone might finally approve a rewire. But that's a budget problem, not a computer problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you're already worried about, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funding, mostly. The association's had its grant cut twice, and there's talk of contracting out repairs to a private firm. If that happens I'd still find work easily, there's loads around here, but I'd lose the pension and the tenants I know.

say: I'd say the money spent on **AI hype** should have gone into **housing**.
At work I'd mostly shrug and get back to **damp and old wiring**.
think: My job is in people's **homes with my hands**, so a chatbot was never a threat.
The bigger risk is Northgate **contracting out** repairs to a private firm.
do: Carry on at **Northgate Homes** and keep the savings ticking over.
Start the **heat pump and solar** course to catch the retrofit work.
feel: **Calm**, because my normal life is pretty good.
S0.quote: My job's in people's homes with my hands, and that was never going to be done by a chatbot.
fieldNote: Dana's worries are about **public funding**, not technology: grant cuts and possible outsourcing.
She sees AI hype as **money diverted** from housing repairs.
Plenty of local work means outsourcing would cost her **the pension and tenants**, not her income.

steps.text: Sign up for the heat pump and solar course for the retrofit programme
Keep doing tenant repairs at Northgate on the same contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say in the union newsletter that the call centre and the admin team need protecting first, because that's who it hits. I'd say the trades are fine for now but we shouldn't be smug. And I'd say any savings should go into fixing homes, not into directors' bonuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine for years. Nobody's sending a robot up a ladder in a damp stairwell in a tower block. What worries me is the tenants, because a lot of them work in shops and call centres, and if they lose their jobs they can't pay rent, and then the association's in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the heat pump course this year. I'd start using the AI tools a bit more for reports and fault notes, once I see the other sparks using them properly. And I'd get the union to negotiate a no-redundancy deal for the admin staff, with retraining into the repairs office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Safe for me, but rough for people I care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Northgate would this hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The contact centre first, definitely. My mate Leanne books all our repairs, and if an AI answers the phone and books the job, that's her gone. Then the planners who sort the job lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: As a rep, what would you actually ask management for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written promise that nobody's made redundant because of AI without a year's notice and a paid retraining place. I'd ask that some of the savings go into the backlog, because there's three hundred homes waiting on electrical work. Whether they'd listen is another matter.

say: I'd say the **call centre and admin** team need protecting first.
Any savings should go into **fixing homes**, not directors' bonuses.
think: Nobody's sending a robot up a ladder in a **damp stairwell** any time soon.
If **tenants** lose shop and call centre jobs, rent arrears hit the association.
do: Do the **heat pump course** this year.
Use **AI tools** more for fault notes once colleagues use them well.
Get the union to push for a **no-redundancy deal** for admin staff.
feel: **Uneasy**, because I'm safe but people I care about aren't.
S1.quote: Nobody's sending a robot up a ladder in a damp stairwell in a tower block.
fieldNote: Dana's concern runs outward: **colleagues** like Leanne in booking and the **tenants'** jobs.
She is pragmatic about AI: she'd **use it** once she sees it proven on her team.
Her ask of management ties savings to the **repairs backlog** of three hundred homes.

steps.text: Finish the heat pump and solar course by next summer
Write fault notes with AI once the other electricians do
Push for a no-redundancy deal for Northgate's admin staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it. I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, fast, because two years is no time for millions of people. In the union I'd be pushing for a national campaign, not just a workplace one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's frightening. The whole booking and planning side goes in 2028, and I reckon the association would cut back to bare repairs. Then by 2031 there's robots that can do a rewire, and I'm thirty-one with a trade that suddenly isn't special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep nine months' money, maybe build it to a year. I'd finish the heat pump course fast, because the retrofit work needs doing before robots are cheap. I'd stand for the union's regional committee, and I'd learn the AI tools properly so I can at least supervise them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got money and I've got a house, but I don't have a plan for after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window. For three years, people like me are still needed to do the hands-on work while the office side gets swallowed. I'd use those years to save, get qualified and get into a role where I'm the one checking the robots, not competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to studying, or try something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if there's a course that leads somewhere. I've thought about becoming an electrical inspector for the council, because someone has to check safety. But honestly, I don't know what jobs would be left by 2031, and I'm not going to pretend I do.

say: I'd say we need something like a **basic income**, fast.
I'd push the union for a **national campaign**, not just a workplace one.
think: The **booking and planning** side goes in 2028, and Northgate cuts back to bare repairs.
By **2031** robots can rewire, and my trade isn't special any more.
do: Build savings from nine months to **a year**.
Finish the **heat pump course** fast to catch retrofit work.
Stand for the union's **regional committee** and learn AI tools to supervise them.
feel: **Anxious**, because I have money and a house but **no plan** after 2031.
S2.quote: For three years, people like me are still needed to do the hands-on work while the office side gets swallowed.
fieldNote: Dana treats the three-year gap as a **window** to save and move into checking work.
She is honest about **not knowing** which jobs survive after 2031.
Her politics push her toward a **national** fight rather than a workplace one.

steps.text: Build savings from nine months of costs to a full year
Finish the heat pump course early for retrofit jobs
Stand for the union's regional committee
Learn the AI fault-finding tools well enough to supervise them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse this time. I'd want councils and housing associations to plan now for retraining tenants and staff. And I'd be telling every young spark I know to get a licence that involves signing off safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means robots around 2034, when I'm thirty-four. That's a lot more breathing room. I think I'd actually get somewhere, maybe into inspection, before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the heat pump course, then the inspector's qualification in year two or three. I'd probably also look at the council job openings. And I'd keep pushing the union on a deal for staff, because the admin side still goes in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not frightened. There's time to make a move, and I'm someone who moves once I've seen it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me watch it first. I'm not an early adopter, I like to see the other sparks try something before I do. Five years gives me time to do that and then follow, and two years doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if it got tough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister, first, and the union. Me and my sister share the house, so we'd never be on the street. My mum would offer, but she needs her money.

say: I'd say we've been **warned**, so there's no excuse this time.
I'd tell young electricians to get a licence that involves **signing off safety**.
think: Robots around **2034** gives me a lot more breathing room.
I'd likely get into **inspection** before the robots arrive.
do: Do the heat pump course, then the **inspector's qualification** in year two or three.
Keep pushing the union for a **staff deal** before admin goes.
feel: **Uneasy**, not frightened, because there's time to move.
S3.quote: Five years lets me watch it first. I'm not an early adopter, I like to see the other sparks try something before I do.
fieldNote: Extra time suits Dana's style: she **follows once proven**, and five years allows that.
Her **shared house** with her sister is her real safety net.
She still keeps a **collective** angle, worried about admin staff.

steps.text: Get the electrical inspector's qualification within three years
Apply for council safety inspector jobs when they open
Keep pushing the union for a retraining deal for admin staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly. I'd want the government to fund retraining properly and keep housing repairs in-house so the jobs stay public. I'd say it in the union and online, calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the softest of the three for me. Robots by 2039, I'm thirty-nine. I'd have time to become an inspector, or move into the planning side of the retrofit programme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the heat pump course now, then inspection, at a normal pace. I'd keep the savings where they are. I'd probably buy my sister out of her half of the house in a few years, so I own something solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mildly. It's a cloud far away, but you can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you do differently than you'd otherwise do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably buy the house outright sooner. And I'd learn the AI tools slowly as they come in, rather than in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a sixteen-year-old thinking about becoming an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do it, but don't stop at the first licence. Get the testing and inspection side, learn the heat pumps, and be the person who knows why things go wrong. I'd tell a sixteen-year-old that the hands are safe for a while, but the head is what keeps you working.

say: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this **fairly**.
I'd want **housing repairs** kept in-house so the jobs stay public.
think: Robots by **2039** leaves time to become an inspector or a **retrofit planner**.
It's the **softest** of the three AGI pictures for me.
do: Do the heat pump course, then **inspection**, at a normal pace.
Buy my **sister's half** of the house within a few years.
feel: Mildly **uneasy**, like a cloud far away that you can still see.
S4.quote: I'd tell a sixteen-year-old that the hands are safe for a while, but the head is what keeps you working.
fieldNote: Dana would make one big **asset move**: buying out her sister's half of the house.
Her advice to young people stresses **diagnosis** and inspection over basic installation.
She'd speak **calmly** in this picture, compared with shouting in the fast one.

steps.text: Take the inspection qualification after the heat pump course
Buy out her sister's half of their nan's house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it leaves no time for anyone, not me, not the tenants, not my mate Leanne in booking. What would help is a properly funded retraining scheme, run by the government with the unions, and a promise that housing repairs stay in public hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the tenants. Everyone talks about workers, but the people I fix things for are the ones with the least cushion. If the shop jobs go, the people living in those flats can't pay rent, and then nobody fixes the wiring at all.

headlineQuote: If the shop jobs go, the people living in those flats can't pay rent, and then nobody fixes the wiring at all.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** in-house electrician at Northgate Homes, a housing association, and a union rep.
She lives in her late nan's house, co-owned with her **sister**, with nine months saved.
She's **pragmatic** about AI and uses it now and then, following once colleagues prove a tool.
Her worries point outward, toward **admin colleagues** and low-paid **tenants**.
More warning time moves her calmly toward **inspection** and retrofit planning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which leaves no time for her, her colleagues or her tenants.
whatWouldHelp: A **government retraining scheme** run with the unions.
